{{short description|African-American biochemist}}

'''Gladys Geraldine Williams Royal''' (August 29, 1926 – November 9, 2002) is one of a small number of early African-American biochemists.<ref name="Diversity">{{cite journal|last1=Johnson-Thompson|first1=Marian C.|author-link=Marian Johnson-Thompson|last2=Jay|first2=James M.|date=1997|title=Ethnic Diversity in ASM: the early history of African-American microbiologists|url=http://www.asm.org/ccLibraryFiles/FILENAME/000000004509/Feb97Johnson-ThompsonFeature.pdf|journal=ASM News|volume=63|issue=2|pages=77–82|accessdate=15 August 2015|via=|archive-date=23 September 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150923175353/http://www.asm.org/ccLibraryFiles/FILENAME/000000004509/Feb97Johnson-ThompsonFeature.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> Part of one of the few African-American husband-and-wife teams in science, Gladys worked with [[George C. Royal]] on research supported by the [[United States Atomic Energy Commission]].  She later worked for many years as principal [[biochemist]] at the Cooperative State Research Service of the  [[U.S. Department of Agriculture]].  Royal was also active in the [[civil rights movement]] in [[Greensboro, North Carolina]].

==Family and early professional career==

Royal Gladys Geraldine Williams was born on August 29, 1926, in [[Dallas, Texas]].<ref name=Brown/> She graduated from [[Dillard University]] with a B.Sc. at the age of 18 in 1944.<ref name=Brown/>  She married [[George C. Royal]] in 1947.<ref name=Brown>{{cite book|last1=Brown|first1=Jeannette E.|title=African American women chemists|date=2012|publisher=Oxford University Press|location=New York|isbn=978-0199742882|pages=49–51|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9jWqBuHb448C&pg=PA49|accessdate=14 August 2015}}</ref>

Royal accompanied her husband to [[Tuskegee, Alabama]], where he taught microbiology in 1947–1948, to Ohio State University and Ohio [[Agricultural experiment station|Agricultural Experiment Station]], where he was a research assistant from 1948 to 1952, and to North Carolina Agricultural and Technical College in Greensboro where he became an assistant professor of [[Bacteriology]] in 1952. At Tuskegee and Ohio State she took classes; by 1953, she was sufficiently qualified to become a professor of chemistry at North Carolina Agricultural and Technical College in Greensboro.<ref name=Brown/><ref name=Team/>

In 1954, Royal received her M.Sc. in [[organic chemistry]] from [[Tuskegee University|Tuskegee]].<ref name=Warren/> She had also taken classes at the [[University of Wisconsin]] and at [[Ohio State University]], from which she received her Ph.D. in 1954.<ref name=Crisis>{{cite journal|title=Statistics: Doctor of Philosophy|journal=The Crisis|date= 1954|volume=61|issue=7|page=417|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=sFcEAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA417}}</ref> Her thesis, ''The  Influence  of  Rations  Containing  Sodium  Acetate  and  Sodium  Propionate  on  the  Composition  of  Tissues  From  Feeder  Lambs'', involved experimental work in [[flavor chemistry]], testing the effects of various feed regimens on the taste of meat.<ref name=PhDThesis>{{cite book|last1=Royal|first1=Gladys|title=The Influence of Rations Containing Sodium Acetate and Sodium Propionate on the Composition of Tissues From Feeder Lambs|date=1954|publisher=The Ohio State University (Ph. D. Dissertation)|location=Columbus, OH}}</ref>

The Royals had six children: George Calvin Royal III,<ref name=Team/> Geraldine Gynnette Royal,<ref name=Team/> Guericke Christopher Royal,<ref name=Team/> jazz musician Gregory Charles Royal,<ref name=Gregory>{{cite web|title=About Gregory Charles Royal|url=http://www.mtv.com/artists/gregory-charles-royal/biography/|website=MTV.com|accessdate=14 August 2015}}{{dead link|date=June 2024|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref> Michelle Renee McNear, and Eric Marcus Royal.

== Research partnership ==
In the late 1950s and early 1960s, the Royals collaborated on important research including that funded by the [[United States Atomic Energy Commission]] involving bone marrow transplants to treat radiation overdoses.<ref name=Warren>{{cite book|last1=Warren|first1=Wini|title=Black women scientists in the United States|date=1999|publisher=Indiana University Press|location=Bloomington, Ind.|isbn=9780253336033|pages=[https://archive.org/details/blackwomenscient00warr/page/249 249]–251|url=https://archive.org/details/blackwomenscient00warr|url-access=registration|accessdate=14 August 2015}}</ref><ref name=College>{{cite news|title=A&T College Receives Grant of $16,915 From U. S. Atomic Energy Commission To Continue Research Begun In 1958|url=http://cdm15116.contentdm.oclc.org/cdm/ref/collection/p15116coll1/id/21883|accessdate=14 August 2015|work=The A. & T. College Register|date=October 2, 1964|archive-date=4 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304130027/http://cdm15116.contentdm.oclc.org/cdm/ref/collection/p15116coll1/id/21883|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=Register>{{cite news|title=A&T Gets Special X-Ray Equipment|url=http://cdm15116.contentdm.oclc.org/cdm/ref/collection/p15116coll1/id/21480|accessdate=14 August 2015|work=The A. & T. College Register|date=13 January 1961|archive-date=4 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304131919/http://cdm15116.contentdm.oclc.org/cdm/ref/collection/p15116coll1/id/21480|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=profs>{{cite news|title=A-T profs awarded U.S. funds for study|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2211&dat=19621117&id=lNMmAAAAIBAJ&sjid=nAIGAAAAIBAJ&pg=4507,4633052&hl=en|accessdate=14 August 2015|work=The Afro American|date= Nov 17, 1962}}</ref> Their work had direct relevance to cancer treatment, which used high doses of radiation and could cause tissue damage. It also reflected [[Cold War]] fears of possible nuclear attack.<ref name="Brown"/>

African-American husband-and-wife teams in science were extremely rare in the early and mid-20th century due to the social, educational and economic climate regarding African Americans in the United States.<ref name=Team>{{cite journal|title=Husband-Wife Team's Project Draws International Interest|journal=Afro-American|date=September 10, 1960|page=10|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2211&dat=19600910&id=W9YmAAAAIBAJ&sjid=4AIGAAAAIBAJ&pg=3170,5118285&hl=en|accessdate=14 August 2015}}</ref><ref name=Davis>{{cite book|last1=Davis|first1=Marianna W.|title=Contributions of Black Women to America|chapter=Physical Chemists|date=1982|publisher=Kenday Press|location=Columbia, SC|pages=446–447|volume=2}}</ref>

The [[United States Atomic Energy Commission|Atomic Energy Commission]] supported at least five grants for funding research on bone marrow transplants, which were proposed jointly by George and Gladys W. Royal.<ref name=Warren/><ref name=profs/> Their work was written and presented at various conferences, including the Fifth International Congress on Nutrition Washington, DC 1960<ref name=Warren/> and the International Congress on Histochemistry and Cytochemistry held in Paris, France in 1960.<ref name=Warren/>

==Later career==
As of 1964, Royal was actively pursuing her interest in flavor chemistry, collaborating with Arthur S. Totten, Associate Professor of Poultry Husbandry at North Carolina Agricultural and Technical College. Newspapers describe their research goal as removing the "tired taste" from chicken. As Royal had done in her Ph.D. research, she examined the use of additive salts on flavor. The research was supported by the North Carolina Experiment Station at Raleigh, NC.<ref name=chicken>{{cite news|title=Team out to add flavor to chicken|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2238&dat=19640818&id=a5YlAAAAIBAJ&sjid=vvQFAAAAIBAJ&pg=717,3063309&hl=en|accessdate=14 August 2015|work=Washington Afro-American|date= August 18, 1964}}</ref>

As of November 6, 1965, the ''Indianapolis Recorder'' reported that Gladys Royal had left the Agricultural and Technical College and joined the [[U.S. Department of Agriculture]], being appointed to "an important research post".  She became the principal biochemist at the Cooperative State Research Service (CSRS), evaluating federal research projects dealing with [[human nutrition]] and consumer use.<ref name="Brown"/><ref name=AGScientist>{{cite news|title=AG SCIENTIST|url=http://indiamond6.ulib.iupui.edu/cdm/ref/collection/IRecorder/id/43475|accessdate=13 October 2015|work=Indianapolis Reporter|date=November 6, 1965}}</ref> Royal served on joint task forces including those for ''A National program of research for food and nutrition'' (1967)<ref name=Joint1967>{{cite book|last1=Joint Task Force of the U.S. Dept. of Agriculture and the State Universities and Land Grant Colleges|title=A National program of research for food and nutrition|date=1967|publisher=Department of Agriculture|location=United States|url=https://archive.org/details/CAT10247705}}</ref> and ''A program of research for the Southern Region in food and nutrition'' (1975).<ref name=Joint1975>{{cite book|last1=Joint Task Force of the Southern Agricultural Experiment Stations and the United States Dept. of Agriculture|title=A program of research for the Southern Region in food and nutrition|date=1975|publisher=Department of Agriculture|location=United States.|url=https://archive.org/details/CAT80742214}}</ref>

== Profession memberships ==
In 1970 Royal became president of the [[Beta Kappa Chi]] scientific society.  She also belonged to [[Sigma Xi]], the [[American Chemical Society]], and the [[American Institute of Chemists]].<ref name="Brown"/>

==Activism==

Royal supported integration at the National convention of the Young Women's Christian Association of the United States of America in 1961,<ref name=YWCA>{{cite book|last1=Young Women's Christian Association of the U.S.A.|title=National convention of the Young Women's Christian Association of the United States of America|date=1961|publisher=National Board, YWCA|location=New York, N.Y.}}</ref> and was involved in inter-racial civil rights activities of the Human Relations Commission of Greensboro, relating to school desegregation in [[Greensboro, North Carolina]].<ref name=Evans>{{cite web|date=1975|title=Oral History Interview with George Evans by William Chafe|url=http://libcdm1.uncg.edu/cdm/ref/collection/CivilRights/id/730|website=Civil Rights Greensboro}}</ref><ref name=Smith>{{cite web|date=1975|title= Oral History Interview with Louise Smith by William Chafe|url=http://libcdm1.uncg.edu/cdm/ref/collection/CivilRights/id/772|website=Civil Rights Greensboro}}</ref> Kay Troxler recalled her as "one of the most capable women I  know".<ref name=Troxler>{{cite web|date=1973|title=Oral History Interview with Kay Troxler by William Chafe|url=http://libcdm1.uncg.edu/cdm/ref/collection/CivilRights/id/782|website=Civil Rights Greensboro}}</ref> Royal also worked with other women to mentor women students and encourage their involvement in science and other fields.<ref name=Stout>{{cite news|title=Allow no ceiling on ambition, Judge Stout advises co-eds|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2238&dat=19640421&id=XJYlAAAAIBAJ&sjid=vvQFAAAAIBAJ&pg=4761,1488669&hl=en|accessdate=13 October 2015|work=Washington Afro-American|date=April 21, 1964}}</ref>

In 1977, she brought suit against the head of the Department of Agriculture and others for "declaratory and injunctive relief and damages for discrimination on account of race". As of February 2, 1977, a decision in ''Royal vs. Bergland'' dismissed the plaintiff's complaints on various technical grounds, "except for plaintiff's claims concerning the failure to promote her to the position of Assistant Deputy Administrator for Family Consumer Services Programs and harassment by the Department of Agriculture".<ref name=Lawsuit>{{cite web|title=Royal v. Bergland, 428 F. Supp. 75 (D.D.C. 1977)|url=http://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/FSupp/428/75/1792613/|accessdate=13 October 2015}}</ref>
